title.en: The Lemon Trees of Cinque Terre

body.markdown: In the terraced gardens above Monterosso, lemon trees grow the way they have for centuries—twisted trunks reaching from stone walls, branches heavy with fruit so fragrant you can smell them from the trail below. My grandmother used to say you could taste the sea in these lemons, the salt air that climbs the cliffs and settles in the leaves.

Walk through any village in early morning and you'll see them everywhere: espaliered against sunny walls, clustered in terra cotta pots, sprawling across terraces that catch the afternoon light. The locals still tend them carefully, protecting the fruit with wooden frames during winter, harvesting with the same deliberate rhythm their grandparents used.

These aren't the massive, uniform lemons you find in supermarkets. Cinque Terre lemons are smaller, thick-skinned, intensely aromatic. Split one open and the oil sprays from the rind—bright, sharp, alive. This is what goes into the limoncino served at family tables, the lemon focaccia cooling in bakery windows, the seafood dishes that taste unmistakably of this place.

You notice them most in spring, when the white blossoms open and the entire hillside seems to exhale sweetness. Bees move between flowers, hikers pause on the Sentiero Azzurro to breathe it in. By summer the fruit hangs golden against dark leaves, and by autumn the harvest begins—hands reaching into branches the same way they've reached for generations, filling baskets to carry down steep paths to village kitchens below.
